analysis.one_liner: Requires big railroads to install collision-preventing train control technology and raises safety fines.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 2008 and never received a committee action, floor vote, or hearing record before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required major freight railroads, railroads with poor safety records, and passenger rail operators to submit plans to the Transportation Secretary for installing positive train control — technology that automatically stops trains before collisions, overspeed derailments, or accidents in work zones [S2] [S3]. It would have required the systems fastest on tracks where commuter and freight trains share rails, barred installation of systems that had failed safety testing, and raised the maximum civil penalties for rail safety violations from as much as $10,000-$20,000 to as much as $25,000-$100,000 [S2] [S3]. It never moved past the referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Rail commuters, intercity passengers, track maintenance workers, and communities along freight and passenger rail corridors. Positive train control is designed to prevent train-to-train collisions, overspeed derailments, work-zone incursions, and trains moving through switches left in the wrong position — the kinds of accidents that kill passengers and railroad workers [S3]. Higher fines give the Safety Secretary more leverage over railroads that underreport accidents or violate hours-of-service limits [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commuters, rail passengers, and track workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires Class I freight railroads, carriers with inadequate safety performance, and intercity or commuter passenger operators to submit — within a year of enactment — an approved plan for implementing positive train control by the end of 2014 [S3].

Requires the systems be implemented no later than the end of 2012 on the highest-risk corridors, which are tracks where commuter and freight trains share rails, and prioritizes corridors carrying hazardous materials or passenger trains [S3].
Raises the statutory civil penalties for rail safety, accident-reporting, and hours-of-service violations from maximums of $10,000 and $20,000 to $25,000 and $100,000 per violation [S3].

Bars installation of any positive train control system or component unless the Secretary certifies it has not experienced a safety-critical failure in prior testing, and lets the Secretary assess civil penalties for missing plan deadlines [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Class I freight railroads and passenger rail operators that would bear the cost of building and installing positive train control systems, and railroads facing steeper fines for safety violations. Those costs would in practice be passed on through freight rates, commuter fares, and government support for passenger rail [S3].

drawbacks.text: Positive train control is an expensive, multi-year technology buildout; the bill gives railroads no funding, so the cost of compliance would land on the industry and flow through to shippers and commuters in the form of higher rates and fares [S3].

The bill prohibits installation of any system or component unless the Secretary certifies it has never experienced a safety-critical failure in testing, a standard so strict that it could slow deployment of the very technology the bill mandates [S3].
Higher per-violation penalties, while modest next to railroad revenues, would be absorbed partly through freight rates passed to businesses and consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — preventing collisions, derailments, and work-zone deaths on shared passenger-freight corridors — is large and directed at the people riding and working on trains. The main costs are real but ordinary regulatory costs: industry-funded technology deployment, higher fines, and a certification gate that could slow rollout. On balance the bill's benefits to rail passengers, workers, and communities near tracks outweigh its costs, though its certification provision is an odd fit for a technology the bill wants deployed quickly.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 110th Congress expired in early January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill for herself and Sen. Barbara Boxer on September 16, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S5].

The bill's central requirement — mandating positive train control — was enacted weeks after introduction in a separate rail safety law that Congress passed and the President signed in October 2008, during the same Congress; this bill itself never advanced. This is well-known public reporting outside the provided sources.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads avoided this bill's compliance timetable and higher fines, though the larger policy outcome did not go their way: Congress mandated positive train control in a separate law within weeks, so the public safety goal was largely achieved through other legislation while this bill sat in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Railroads, briefly; a parallel law passed instead

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring positive train control plans and higher rail safety penalties and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the bill received no hearing, markup, or vote after its September 2008 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only recorded supporters were two Democratic senators from California, so the partisan shape of the opposition is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to fund and install positive train control by 2014, faster on high-risk corridors, and raised their maximum safety fines from $10,000-$20,000 to $25,000-$100,000 per violation [S3]. Their compliance costs flow through to shippers, but the mandate targets safety failures that harm passengers, workers, and communities [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Intercity and commuter passenger rail operators
industries.note: The bill would have obligated them to submit positive train control plans and implement systems by the end of 2012 on shared commuter-freight track — the corridors where their passengers face the greatest collision risk [S2] [S3]. They would bear implementation costs but are also the most direct beneficiaries of collision-prevention technology.

A mandate for every Class I railroad and passenger operator to build positive train control plans and certified systems would have created a large market for signaling and control technology, with the Secretary's certification gate shaping which products could be installed [S3].
